newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's lumber sector sees 1997-98 price slump.
newsitem.headline: Canada's lumber sector sees 1997-98 price slump.

text.p: Canada's softwood lumber industry executives expect sharply lower prices for their products in 1997-98 as North American demand weakens, an industry conference was told on Thursday.
In a speech to the Canadian Lumbermen's Association, Leo Huard, president of the industry group, said lumber prices in 1997 would be volatile.
"According to a recent survey, industry analysts expect the price of lumber to vary between US$340 and US$390 per 1,000 board feet in 1997," Huard said.
Huard was quoting prices for the benchmark spruce two-by-four, which peaked above US$450 in November 1996.

Huard said analysts forecast prices reaching their 1997 peak in April, the first anniversary of the contentious Canada-U.S. lumber agreement, which set an annual quota on Canadian softwood lumber exports to the United States.

Bernard Fuller, an analyst with Resource Information Systems Inc, of Bedford, Massachusetts, told the conference that prices for spruce two-by-fours could drop to US$300 per 1,000 board feet or lower as the North American market reached a cyclical trough in 1998.
Fuller said prices would decline because of lackluster growth in demand, rapid capacity expansion in low-cost regions and lumber products, and substitution between wood products.
"Prices and profits in this environment will be under significant downward pressure," Fuller said.

Fuller said he expected an important demand component -- total U.S. housing starts, including single-family dwelling contruction, apartments and mobile homes -- to slip to about 1.5 million in 1997 and slightly lower in 1998 from 1.8 million units in 1996.
U.S. softwood lumber consumption was forecast to decline to about 43 billion board feet in 1998-99 from an estimated record of more than 50 billion board feet in 1996, he said.

Fuller said lumber prices would also be skewed by the Canada-U.S. trade pact on softwood lumber, which on April 1, 1996 set an annual quota of 14.7 billion board feet on the volume of softwood lumber exports to the United States from the Canadian provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and Quebec.
Shipments above the quota will be hit with tariffs of US$50 and US$100 per thousand board feet.

Fuller said the quota had raised average lumber prices in the United States to the point where some home builders were willing to consider switching to substitutes such as steel. Current market conditions appeared to be hurting British Columbia lumber exporters most, Fuller said.

Partly due to higher stumpage fees in the Western Canadian province and other factors, British Columbia lumber companies had joined the ranks of North America's highest-cost producers from among the lowest-cost. That placed lumber companies in Alberta, Quebec and the Canadian Maritimes at a cost advantage, he said.
"On average, eastern Canada producers could swallow the US$100 duty, not pass it on to customers, and still make money," Fuller said.
